analysis.one_liner: Directs the FTC to investigate whether oil companies' conduct inflated gas prices for consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2023 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no further action and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to use its existing investigative powers to study whether oil and gas companies engaged in anti-competitive, collusive, or price-gouging conduct — including whether companies kept prices high by cutting production, buying back their own stock, or restricting alternative fuels. The FTC, working with state attorneys general, would report findings and recommendations to Congress annually for three years. It also authorizes $15 million a year for two years and up to 50 new FTC staff to do the work.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households paying for gasoline, who would get an official, detailed accounting of whether high prices at the pump reflect market competition or company conduct. The FTC gains resources and a clear mandate to examine the industry, and state attorneys general get a federal partner in the investigation.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FTC to investigate anti-competitive, collusive, or other conduct in oil and gas markets, including the actual price consumers pay.

The study must specifically examine whether companies reduced fuel supply — including cutting production investment or engaging in stock buybacks — and whether conduct inflated consumer costs or constituted price gouging.
The FTC must report results and recommendations to Congress annually for three years, with state attorneys general participating where appropriate.
Authorizes $15 million per year for fiscal 2024 and 2025 and up to 50 additional FTC personnel to carry out the study.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, whose pricing, investment, and stock-buyback decisions would face federal scrutiny and possible recommendations for new regulation. Taxpayers fund the authorized $30 million total for the investigation, and the FTC takes on the staffing and reporting workload.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies, plus taxpayers funding the study

drawbacks.text: It is a study, not enforcement: the bill would produce reports and recommendations but would not cap prices, break up companies, or directly stop any conduct, so consumers would see no immediate relief even if gouging were found.

The bill costs money — $15 million authorized for each of fiscal 2024 and 2025 — and expands FTC staffing, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is a real expense for an investigation with uncertain results.
Adding up to 50 personnel 'without regard to the civil service laws' sidesteps standard federal hiring rules, a process concern an opponent could raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For $30 million over two years, the public would get a detailed, official answer to one of the most persistent cost-of-living questions — whether gas prices reflect competition or company conduct. That is a modest, targeted expenditure, but the bill's design limits its value: it produces findings and recommendations only, so any actual relief would depend on later legislation that may never come. The honest weighing is that it is a reasonable first step with no guarantee of follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2023, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on January 25, 2023, with Senator Ben Ray Luján.
After introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the only action the bill ever received.
The bill had one cosponsor and no further committee or floor action through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies avoided the FTC investigation into their pricing, production, and stock-buyback conduct, and consumers never got the official accounting the bill promised.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on January 25, 2023.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (118th Congress)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in January 2023 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving it to die when Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats, and no Republicans signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would subject the industry's pricing, production cuts, and stock buybacks to a dedicated FTC investigation, with findings that could support later regulation. An investigation into whether company conduct inflates pump prices puts the industry's interest directly at odds with consumers' interest in cheaper gas.

The FTC would receive $15 million a year, up to 50 new staff, and an explicit mandate to examine oil and gas markets — resources the bill's backers saw as strengthening the agency's consumer-protection work.
